title: Absolute, Relative and Percentage Error — Year 9

header.title: Absolute, Relative and Percentage Error
header.subtitle: How wrong is wrong? Every measurement is an estimate

meta.lesson-focus: Calculate absolute error |measured − exact|, relative error (absolute error ÷ exact value), and percentage error; use absolute value notation in the error formula; recognise that all measurements are estimates with associated uncertainty.
meta.ac9-descriptor-text: calculate and interpret absolute, relative and percentage errors in measurements, recognising that all measurements are estimates
meta.sa-conceptual-understanding: Calculations are affected by sources of error and should be interpreted in the context of the problem

html.section0_intro: Today is all about comparing an estimate with the true value. These three questions check the subtraction and percentage skills you need.
html.section_warmup:
A real situation that is secretly today's measurement.

The Year 9 formal committee estimated 250 guests and paid the caterer $40 a head in advance. On the night, 200 guests turned up.

They were out by 50 people, which cost $2000 in wasted meals. Is "out by 50" a big mistake? For a stadium of 50 000 it would be tiny. For a formal of 200 it is huge.

The gap between the estimate and the true value is the absolute error (50 people). Comparing it with the true value gives the percentage error: 50200 × 100% = 25%. Today you learn to calculate both, and why every measurement you ever make carries some error.
html.vocab_cards:
Exact vs measured value
Tap to flip
The exact value is the true (or actual) amount. The measured value is the estimate, reading or prediction.
Actual guests 200; estimate 250.
Absolute value |x|
Tap to flip
The distance from zero, so it is never negative.
|−6| = 6 and |6| = 6.
Absolute error
Tap to flip
How far the measurement is from the exact value: |measured − exact|.
|250 − 200| = 50 guests.
Relative error
Tap to flip
The absolute error as a fraction of the exact value: absolute errorexact value.
50200 = 0.25
Percentage error
Tap to flip
The relative error written as a percentage: relative error × 100%.
0.25 × 100% = 25%

📏 Estimate (measured)

💡 Counting whole things and definitions can be exact. Every measurement is an estimate: a ruler, scale or stopwatch can only be read to its smallest mark, so there is always some error.
html.section4_heading: Match each term to its formula or value
html.worked_example:
The formal committee estimated 250 guests; 200 actually came. Find the absolute error, the relative error and the percentage error of the estimate.

1
Name the exact value, then find the absolute error
The exact value is what really happened: 200 guests. The estimate is the "measured" value.
Absolute error = |measured − exact| = |250 − 200| = 50 guests
2
Relative error: divide by the EXACT value
Compare the error with the true size of the event, not with the estimate.
Relative error = absolute errorexact value = 50200 = 0.25
3
Percentage error = relative error × 100%
Check it makes sense: 50 is a quarter of 200, so 25% is reasonable.
0.25 × 100% = 25%
Trap: 50250 × 100% = 20% divides by the estimate. That is wrong.
Answer Absolute error 50 guests  ·  relative error 0.25  ·  percentage error 25%
html.we_do_intro: A ruler measures a pencil as 14.4 cm. Precise digital calipers give its exact length as 15 cm. Work through each prompt with a partner, then we check as a class.
html.strategy_section:
★Spot the mistake

A student has worked out a percentage error but made a mistake. Read each line carefully, then click the line where the mistake first appears.

A weather app forecast a maximum of 32 °C. The actual maximum was 40 °C. Find the percentage error of the forecast.
1 Absolute error = |32 − 40| = 8 °C
2 Relative error = 832 = 0.25
3 Percentage error = 0.25 × 100% = 25%

✓ Right: that's where the mistake first appears.

Why: the student divided by the forecast (32). The forecast is the estimate; the exact value is what really happened, 40 °C. Relative error = absolute errorexact value = 840. Line 1 is fine: |32 − 40| = |−8| = 8.

Now type the correct relative error for line 2 as a decimal:

★Hinge check 🎯 Pick one

A certified 1000 g test weight is placed on a cheap kitchen scale. The scale reads 950 g. What is the percentage error of the scale?

Percentage error = |measured − exact|exact × 100% = ?
That's the absolute error, not a percentage. The scale is out by 50 g. To turn that into a percentage you still divide by the exact value (1000 g) and multiply by 100%.
You divided by the measured value. 50950 × 100% ≈ 5.3% compares the error with the scale's reading. Always divide by the exact value, 1000 g.
Correct. Absolute error = |950 − 1000| = 50 g. Relative error = 501000 = 0.05. Percentage error = 0.05 × 100% = 5%.
You stopped at the relative error. 501000 = 0.05 is the relative error. Multiply by 100% to get the percentage error.

weDo.q: (a) Absolute error = |14.4 − 15| = ___ cm. (Type the number only: no units, no % sign.)
weDo.hint: 14.4 − 15 = −0.6, and the absolute value of −0.6 is 0.6.

fb.-0.6: Absolute error uses |…|, so it is never negative.

weDo.q: (b) Relative error = absolute error ÷ exact value = ___ (decimal).

fb.0.6: That is the absolute error. Now divide it by the exact value, 15.

weDo.q: (c) Percentage error = ___ %. (Type the number only: no units, no % sign.)

checkpoint.q: The canteen expected to sell 80 pies. It actually sold 100. What is the percentage error of the expectation? (Type the number only: no units, no % sign.)

fb.25: You divided by the estimate (80). Divide by the exact value: what actually happened.

checkpoint.q: A rod is exactly 40 cm long. A student measures it as 41 cm. What is the relative error, as a decimal?

fb.1: That is the absolute error. Divide it by the exact value, 40.

practice1.q: Exact value 50, measured value 47. Absolute error?

fb.-3: Absolute error uses absolute value, so it is never negative.

The absolute error is 4 and the exact value is 80. Relative error, as a decimal?
A relative error is 0.03. What is the percentage error? (Type the number only: no units, no % sign.)

fb.0.03: That is the relative error. Multiply by 100 to make it a percentage.

practice1.q: A bag of rice is exactly 200 g. The scale reads 190 g. Percentage error? (Type the number only: no units, no % sign.)

fb.10: 10 g is the absolute error. Divide by 200, then multiply by 100%.

practice1.q: A field is exactly 25 m wide. A student paces it out as 24 m. Percentage error? (Type the number only: no units, no % sign.)
A 60 s timer is checked with a stopwatch, which reads 63 s. Percentage error of the stopwatch reading? (Type the number only: no units, no % sign.)
A runner's exact time is 12.5 s. A hand-held stopwatch gives 12.0 s. Percentage error? (Type the number only: no units, no % sign.)
A jug holds exactly 400 mL; it is measured as 410 mL. Relative error as a decimal (or fraction)?

fb.10: That is the absolute error. Divide by the exact value, 400.

practice2.q: Organisers predicted 1200 people at a concert. 1500 came. Percentage error of the prediction? (Type the number only: no units, no % sign.)

fb.25: You divided by the prediction. The exact value is the number who actually came.

practice2.q: Without absolute value, the signed error = estimate − exact. A forecast says 30 mm of rain; 36 mm falls. What is the signed error, in mm?
practice2.hint: 30 − 36 = −6. The minus sign shows the forecast was too low.

fb.6: 6 is the absolute error. Signed error keeps the sign: estimate − exact.

practice2.q: In the rain question, a negative signed error means the forecast was an over- or under-estimate? Type over or under.
practice2.hint: Estimate − exact is negative when the estimate is smaller than the exact value.

practice2.q: A packet's exact mass is 350 g and the measurement has a percentage error of 2%. What is the absolute error, in g?

fb.343: 343 g is a possible reading. The question asks for the absolute error itself.

practice2.q: A 2.5 m pole is measured by Ana as 2.45 m and by Ben as 2.6 m. Who measured more accurately? Type Ana or Ben.
practice2.hint: Ana's error: 0.05 m. Ben's error: 0.1 m. Smaller error = more accurate.

practice2.q: A 10 cm pencil and a 1 m (100 cm) bench are each measured with an error of 1 cm. What is the percentage error for the pencil? (Type the number only: no units, no % sign.)
practice2.hint: 1 ÷ 10 = 0.1 = 10%. (The bench: 1 ÷ 100 = 1%. Same absolute error, very different percentage error.)

fb.1: 1% is the bench. For the pencil, divide 1 by 10.

practice3.q: A formal committee under-estimated: 400 guests came and their estimate had a percentage error of 10%. Meals cost $50 each and were ordered for the estimate. How much extra (in $) must be paid for the missing meals?

fb.40: 40 is the number of missing meals. Multiply by the $50 cost.

practice3.q: The Year 9 camp was budgeted at $12 000. The actual cost was $12 500. Percentage error of the budget? (Type the number only: no units, no % sign.)

fb.4.17: You divided by the budget. Divide by the actual (exact) cost.

practice3.q: An estimate of 0.75 kg was an under-estimate by 0.05 kg. Percentage error? (Type the number only: no units, no % sign.)

fb.6.67: You divided by the estimate. First find the exact value: 0.75 + 0.05.

practice3.q: A beam must be exactly 3.5 m long. The builder accepts a percentage error of at most 2%. What is the longest beam (in m) that is still acceptable?

fb.0.07: 0.07 m is the largest allowed absolute error. Add it to 3.5 m.

exitProbs.hint: Absolute error 100. Divide by the exact value, 1000.
